$comment: Thresholds for the balance gate. `npm run sim` and `npm run check:balance` read this file and
turn the measured numbers into PASS / FAIL / SKIP. Nothing here is hard-coded in the scripts.
Three rules this file exists to enforce:
1. A check whose sample is too small SKIPS loudly. It is never counted as a pass.
2. A threshold left null means 'not decided yet' and also SKIPS. It never silently passes.
3. Unknown keys are a hard load error, so a typo cannot quietly disable a check.
Mana cost is frozen (see README). Nothing in here is a licence to change a card's cost.
Minimum evidence each check needs before it is allowed to have an opinion.
Below these numbers the check reports SKIP with the reason, and the run's verdict says so.
How often the player who moves first wins. 50% is a perfectly fair start.
Band widened from 45-55 to 44-56 on owner ruling: the game measures 46-49%, and a 45%
floor sits close enough to that to go red on shuffle luck rather than on a real problem.
Median duel length in player-turns (about half that many turns each).
The shipped game measures 21. Outside this band the pacing has moved and every
per-turn effect in the game changed value with it (README, Choosing a pacing lever).

softLocks.$comment: A live game that offers nobody a legal move. Always a bug. No tolerance, no sample floor.

stalls.$comment: A duel that hit the turn cap without anybody winning. No tolerance, no sample floor.

$comment: Breaches found by the fuzzer: crashes, NaN or negative stats, duplicate minions,
a save that will not survive a JSON round trip. No tolerance.
NOTE ON COVERAGE: the full invariant suite runs on every fuzz duel, but on only every
40th self-play duel (deepChecks in simulate.ts) because it is ~3x slower. So a corrupt
state that only competent play can assemble is checked in a fraction of the bot duels.
Duels where both cores fall at once, so nobody wins. Not a stall and not a soft-lock.
This check exists because an adversarial review pointed out that a draw silently leaves
every other rate here measured on a smaller sample - the coin flip, the ladder and the
snowball metric all just quietly exclude it - so the game could start ending in draws
half the time with no lamp lighting anywhere. Measured at 0 on the shipped game; 0.5% is
a guard that tolerates the genuinely rare mutual kill without tolerating a trend.
How often a player can play NOTHING across their first N own turns — measured by asking
the engine for legal moves, not by comparing costs, so The Coin, discounts and relics count.
Owner ruling: gate on the 3-turn window (the real pathology). The turn-1 number is reported
beside it but never gated — going first means two cards and one mana, so a dead first turn
is the design, not a defect.
LATEST FULL RUN on 2000 openings at the current hand sizes of 3 and 3: 14.3% overall
(286 openings). Re-baselined after the opening-hand change; the earlier 17.3% measurement
used 2 and 3 cards, while the older 24% guard was based on hand sizes of 1 and 2.
Owner ruling: accept up to 18%. This is deliberately close to the measured 17.3% baseline.
Re-baseline this again after any change to hand size, the draw, or the cost curve.
Does skill actually win? Each matchup is its own check, so the summary names which one broke.
A matchup passes only when BOTH hold: the observed rate clears its floor, AND the 95%
confidence interval sits entirely above 50% — i.e. the gap is real, not shuffle luck.
Measured on the shipped cheat bot, 2026-08-17, at these sample sizes: hard>easy 91.0,
hard>normal 82.0, normal>easy 71.5.
Sample sizes are per matchup because the cost and the need are inverted. A duel involving
the hard bot takes about eight times as long (it searches whole turns), and those two
matchups have 25-point margins that need almost no sample: at 100 duels the chance of a
false red is far under one in a thousand. normal>easy has the least headroom over its floor
and is the cheap matchup, so it gets 200. Flat 200s across all three would cost roughly
16 minutes and buy nothing.
Raising a sample is the WRONG tool for comparing two runs. Every ladder duel is seeded by
matchup and index, so two runs deal identical shuffles; `--ladder-compare` pairs them game
by game and counts only the results that flipped, which cancels shuffle luck entirely. That
sees a 4-point change at 100 duels, where subtracting two percentages would need about 900.
Take whoever is ahead at turn N and ask how often they go on to win. A game already
decided at turn 5 feels bad for the ten turns it still takes to end.
'Ahead' = ahead on core health AND on board strength at the same time. Measured all three
ways and gated on that one, because health alone turned out to be a poor signal this early:
the player on more health at turn 5 is often just the one who has not attacked yet.
Duels where the two measures disagree are excluded, not counted as ties.
MEASURED across 627 duels with a clear turn-5 leader: 59.5%. The curve then runs 66% at
turn 9, 73% at turn 13, 85% at turn 17 — a game that tightens gradually rather than one
decided in its opening. This is a genuinely healthy result.
70 is a regression guard with room for normal variation (about five standard errors above
the measured value). The line where an early lead starts to FEEL deterministic is nearer 80.
Report-only tuning. Nothing under here can fail the gate.
watchlistPlayRatePct: the owner's real signal for cards that rot in hand. The worst card in
the roster is played 16% of the times it is drawn, so a 1% gate would never fire; 20% is
where the interesting cards actually sit (owner ruling — the 1% gate was dropped for this).
tierOutlier*: a card is only named as an outlier when it is BOTH beyond this many standard
errors from its own cost tier's mean AND at least this many points away from it. Judging
against the tier, never the roster average (README, Reading the measured numbers).
diffNoiseMultiple: a before/after card delta is marked 'noise' unless it exceeds this many
standard errors of the difference. At default sample sizes that floor is around 12 points,
which is the honest resolution of a per-card diff.
